content: Dry eyes occur when there is an insufficient production of tears. Tears are essential for maintaining proper lubrication of the eyes and for removing debris and foreign particles. Symptoms of Dry Eyes: If you have dry eyes, you may experience a burning, scratching, or stinging sensation. Your eyes may feel strained or fatigued, especially after reading, even for short periods. Contact lens wearers may find their lenses uncomfortable. Prolonged dry eyes can result in small abrasions on the surface of the eyes. Causes of Dry Eyes: Common causes of dry eyes include: Aging Exposure to dry environments or workplaces, such as those with wind or air conditioning Sun exposure Smoking or exposure to second-hand smoke Use of cold or allergy medications Eye injuries or conditions affecting the eyes or eyelids, such as drooping eyelids or bulging eyes Sjogren's syndrome, which is characterized by dryness of the eyes, mouth, and mucous membranes, often accompanied by rheumatoid arthritis or other joint disorders Previous eye surgeries When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: You should contact your healthcare provider if: Your eyes are red or painful. You notice flaking, discharge, or lesions on your eyes or eyelids. You have experienced trauma to the eye, or you have bulging eyes or drooping eyelids. You experience joint pain, swelling, or stiffness. You also have a dry mouth. Your dry eyes do not improve with self-care measures after a few days. Treatment Options: The following measures may help alleviate dry eyes: Use artificial tears, available as drops or ointments. Ointments provide longer-lasting relief but may cause blurry vision due to their thicker consistency. Avoid smoking and exposure to second-hand smoke, direct wind, and air conditioning. Use a humidifier, particularly during the winter months. Make a conscious effort to blink more frequently. Rest your eyes regularly. Medical Evaluation and Diagnosis: Your healthcare provider will take a detailed medical history and perform a physical examination, including a thorough eye examination. To better understand your condition, they may ask questions such as: How long have you had dry eyes? Does it affect one or both eyes? Is the dryness constant, or does it occur only at specific times, during certain activities, or in particular environments? Does the dryness seem related to wind, dust, chemicals, sunlight, or light exposure? Does it affect your vision or cause pain? Do your eyelids close completely and easily? Have you noticed any drainage from your eyes? Are there factors that worsen or improve your dry eyes? Have you tried artificial tears, and do they provide relief? Are you taking any medications? If so, which ones? Have you had any surgeries or injuries involving your eyes or nose? Do you have allergies? Have you started using any new cosmetics? Do you experience other symptoms, such as dry mouth or joint discomfort? Your healthcare provider may also perform specific tests to evaluate tear production and diagnose dry eyes. Artificial tears or other treatments may be prescribed based on the findings.
